39-001.r: Rise of the Marathas → religious consciousness, geographical security, political awakening and high-quality leadership (all of the above).

39-002.r: Shaded map in this question → territory ruled by the Marathas.

39-003.r: Shivaji defeated the Mughals at Salher (1672 A.D.); born 1627 (or 1630) at Shivneri Fort; took title 'Chhatrapati' at his coronation, 1674.

39-005.r: Bijapur commander sent to crush Shivaji in 1659 → Afzal Khan, who was killed by Shivaji.

39-006.r: Shivaji escaped Mughal custody from → Agra (Jaipur Bhawan), where Aurangzeb kept him under house arrest in 1666 A.D.

39-007.r: Shivaji's capital → Raigarh; crowned 'Chhatrapati' in 1674 A.D. by Vishveshwar (Gaga Bhatt) of Banaras, who declared him Kshatriya.

39-009.r: Shivaji formally crowned Chhatrapati → Raigarh, 1674 A.D.; ceremony performed by Gaga Bhatta (Vishweshwar) of Varanasi.

39-010.r: Shivaji's Guru → Samarth Ramdas, author of the Advaita text 'Daasbodh' and the poem 'Shivastuti'.

39-011.r: Shivaji chronology → Fort of Chakan won (1648) – clash with Mughals begins (1657) – Afzal Khan episode (1659) – sack of Surat (1664).

39-012.r: Ashtapradhan → Shivaji's council of eight ministers: Peshwa (PM), Amatya (finance), Mantri (interior), Sachiv (letters), Sumant (foreign), Senapati, Pandit Rao (priest), Nyayadhish (justice).

39-022.r: Shivaji was advised by the Ashtapradhan, but it was no cabinet: ministers headed departments as his secretaries and he could reject advice; A true, R false.

39-023.r: Big Deshmukhs opposed Shivaji → they wanted to stay feudal lords under Bijapur, keeping autonomy and privileges; A and R true, R explains A.

39-024.r: Shivaji's silver coins → Rupaya, Lari and Taka; Ruka was a coin of the Kakatiya dynasty.

39-025.r: Streamlined Maratha administration after Sambhaji → Balaji Vishwanath; from November 1713 power passed from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwas.

39-026.r: Peshwas in order → Balaji Vishwanath (1713-1720) – Bajirao I (1720-1740) – Balaji Bajirao (1740-1761) – Madhavrao (1761-1772).

39-027.r: Peshwa order → Balaji Vishwanath – Bajirao I – Balaji Bajirao – Madhav Rao I.
39-027.h: B-B-B-M: three B's, then Madhav Rao.

39-028.r: Peshwas → Balaji Vishwanath (1713-1720) – Bajirao I (1720-1740) – Madhav Rao I (1761-1772) – Narayan Rao (1772-1773).

39-029.r: Peshwas → Balaji Vishwanath (1713-20) – Balaji Bajirao (1740-61) – Narayan Rao (1772-73) – Raghunath Rao 'Raghoba' (1773-74).

39-030.r: Maratha rulers → Sambhaji (1680-1689) – Rajaram (1689-1700) – Shivaji II (1700-1708) – Chhatrapati Shahuji (1708-1749, Sambhaji's son).

39-031.r: By 1750 the Peshwa headed the Maratha Confederacy (Sangola agreement, 1750); post hereditary from Balaji Bajirao (1740); A and R true, R explains A.

39-033.r: Marathas → strongest native power after Mughal decline, but never developed a concept of a united Indian nation; A true, R false.

39-034.r: Maratha leader at Aurangzeb's death → Tarabai, Rajaram's widow, fighting the Mughals on behalf of her son Shivaji-II.

39-035.r: Tara Bai → regent for minor son Shivaji-II after Rajaram; led the struggle against Mughals from 1700 A.D.; retook Singhgarh, Raigarh and Satara.

39-036.r: Saranzami system → Maratha feudal-military land grant to Jagirdars for maintaining forts and troops (Maratha land revenue system).

39-037.r: Chauth → Maratha claim of revenue for protection, collected from 'Mughalai' provinces.

39-038.r: Eyewitness historian of Third Battle of Panipat (14th January 1761) → Kashiraj Pandit: 'catastrophic for Marathas' (Sadashivrao Bhau vs Abdali).

39-039.r: Immediate cause of Abdali's invasion (Panipat III) → revenge for the Marathas expelling his viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore.

39-040.r: Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761) → Afghans under Ahmad Shah Abdali crushed the Marathas led by Sadashivrao Bhau.

39-045.r: Rohilla confidant of Abdali → Najib Khan (Najib-ud-Daulah), made his chief agent and Mir Bakshi after Abdali looted Delhi (January 1757).

39-046.r: Modi script → used by the Marathas, especially for revenue and administrative records.

40-001.r: Aurangzeb's successor (1707) → his son Muazzam (Shah Alam), aged sixty-three, as Bahadur Shah; ruled 1707-1712.

40-002.r: Jahandar Shah → first unfit Mughal, raised by Amir Zulfiqar Khan; defeated and killed by nephew Farrukh Siyar, February 1713; called 'lewd Moron'.

40-003.r: Duty-free trade in Bengal for the English → Farrukh Siyar's decree of 1717 A.D., on paying an annual tax of 3000.

40-004.r: 'King Makers' → Sayyid brothers Hussain Ali and Abdullah (1713-1720): made Farrukh Siyar king (1713), deposed him (1719), then raised Rafi-ud-darjat, Rafi-ud-daula, Muhammad Shah.

40-005.r: Last Mughal on the Peacock Throne (Mayur Singhasan/Takht-i-Taus) → Muhammad Shah (1719-1748); Nadir Shah took it and the Kohinoor after Karnal (1739).

40-007.r: Nadir Shah invaded India → 1739 AD: Battle of Karnal and sack of Delhi.

40-008.r: Eunuchs and ladies dominated the court → Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' (1719-48), obsessed with wine, beauty and animal fights.

40-010.r: Chronology → Jahandar Shah (1712-13) – Muhammad Shah (1719-1748) – Ahmad Shah (1748-54) – Alamgir II (1754-1759).

40-011.r: Chronology → Bahadur Shah-I (1707-1712) – Jahandar Shah (1712-1713) – Farrukhsiyar (1713-1719) – Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela' (1719-1748).

40-012.r: Emperor kept out of Delhi by Wazir Ghaziuddin → Shah Alam II (Ali Gauhar, 1759-1806); entered Delhi with Maratha help in 1772; English took Delhi in 1803.

40-013.r: Last Mughal Bahadur Shah Zafar (1837-57) → son of Akbar-II; British pensioner at the Red Fort; died 1862.

40-015.r: Not correct → Zafar got one lakh rupees a month (Rs. 99000 in Delhi plus one thousand in Lucknow); true: Zauq and Ghalib taught him, Hasan Askari guided him.
